newsitem.title: POLAND: SOCCER-PIECHNICZEK LOOKS FOR SUCCESS SECOND TIME ROUND.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PIECHNICZEK LOOKS FOR SUCCESS SECOND TIME ROUND.

text.p: Poland's place in next year's World Cup finals and the future of national coach Antoni Piechniczek are on the line when England provide the opposition for a vital qualifier on Saturday.
Piechniczek, who took control of the national team for the second time a year ago, knows all about success at this level.
During his first spell in charge he took Poland to third place in the 1982 finals in Spain and into the finals in Mexico in 1986.

He later coached the national teams of Tunisia and the United Arab Emirates but returned to take over Poland again last summer after the unsuccessful reign of Henryk Apostel and the short, unhappy six-month tenancy of Wladyslaw Stachurski.
Right now Piechniczek's past successes are being overlooked and instead he has been heavily criticised for constantly changing line-ups.

He badly needs a win in Chorzow on Saturday to quiet ever-louder voices calling for his dismissal. "The present national squad doesn't have character -- and plays with no character -- perhaps a different coach is needed," Grzegorz Lato, the most capped player in Polish soccer history, told Pilka Nozna Plus football monthly recently.
If Poland lose on Saturday they will be eliminated from next year's finals. Victory would leave them with a chance of reaching the playoffs.

Poland's frantic effort to reach their first major finals since the Mexico World Cup 11 years ago is in stark contrast to their successes of the 1970s and early 1980s when their teams blended style and uncompromising, solid discipline in equal measure.

The first hint of their potential came when they won the 1972 Olympic tournament and many of that team carried the country towards the 1974 World Cup. Their place was secured on a memorable night in London when they held England to a 1-1 draw at Wembley and goalkeeper Jan Tomaszewski played the game of his life to deny England time and again.
The stars of that side -- Kazimierz Deyna, Robert Gadocha, Andrzej Szarmach and tournament top scorer Lato up front -- Wladyslaw Zmuda and Jerzy Gorgon in defence -- impressed in Germany.

In 1978 they were eliminated by Brazil in the second round, but in 1982, inspired by the outstanding ginger-haired Zbigniew Boniek, they again reached the last four where they lost 2-0 to Italy in the semifinals. A 3-2 win over France in the playoff secured third place for the second time in eight years.
Since then Poland's impact on the international scene has been minimal.

The country's football establishment are split over the reasons for the fall from grace. Some say the talent is no longer there, while others blame out-of-date training methods and inadequate organisation.
"We lack outstanding talent and sometimes you have to wait a generation to produce such players," Zbigniew Kalinowski, the deputy head of the Polish Football Association told Reuters.
"Many have left to play abroad and the coach doesn't see them so much. The motivation is not what it used to be," he said.

The average salary in the Polish first division is roughly 10,000 zlotys ($3,000) a month and while the better players can earn vastly more abroad, it leaves the domestic league lacking in true talent.
Domestic league games, watched by small crowds, are no longer the place for emerging stars to shine or for players to be motivated.
Commentator Waldemar Lodzinski highlights the key problem of Polish clubs -- they have to sell their stars to survive.

"Clubs need to transfer as many good players as possible because the transfers are their main source of income and this does little to develop individual or team character or keep players in club teams motivated," he said.

It's a problem that is shared by many other countries in eastern Europe including Romania, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic, all of whom have tasted international success of varying degrees in the last few years.

And while Poland cannot currently boast a star like Bulgarian Hristo Stoichkov or Romanian Gheorghe Hagi, it does possess good strikers such as Marek Citko and Cezary Kucharski, who have both been coveted by foreign clubs but are still playing in Poland.
Nevertheless, Lodzinski is unimpressed and feels that Piechniczek must change his methods in order to ignite a new spark in Polish soccer.

Piechniczek's open hostility to giving overseas players key roles in the national team is well known. His argument is that if they cannot get back for his week-long get-togethers and training camps he cannot build a team around them.

"This idea must change. The demanding schedules of many foreign club players make those strict old-style organisational methods ineffective and keep some of our best players on the bench," Lodzinski said.
A victory against England on Saturday could just herald the start of a new era of success but defeat would keep Poland in the wilderness for the foreseeable future.
